sources.section: Diarrhea and dehydration — oral rehydration solution
sources.text:
Diarrhea kills mainly through dehydration, especially in children. **The main measure is to replace fluids.**

**Homemade solution (when oral rehydration salts – ORS – from a pharmacy/clinic are not available):**

- **1 liter of drinking water** (boiled and cooled, or treated)
- **6 level teaspoons of sugar** (~25–30 g)
- **½ level teaspoon of salt** (~2.5 g)

Mix well. It should taste no saltier than tears. Offer small, frequent sips after each bowel movement. Make a fresh batch every 24 hours.

- Keep feeding (and breastfeeding babies).
- **Children:** the WHO recommends **zinc** for 10–14 days along with ORS (dose according to age and package insert).
- Signs of severe dehydration: very drowsy, sunken eyes, skin that is slow to go back when pinched, unable to drink, no urine. **Seek urgent care.**
- Diarrhea with blood, high fever or lasting more than 2 weeks also needs evaluation.

> Sources: WHO/UNICEF — *Oral Rehydration Salts: production of the new ORS* (2006) and *Clinical management of acute diarrhoea* (2004); Werner, D. — *Onde Não Há Médico* (*Where There Is No Doctor*), "rehydration drink". Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — management of acute diarrhea.

sources.title: Oral rehydration therapy
sources.text:
Oral rehydration therapy

Oral rehydration therapy
An oral rehydration solution (250ml) prepared according to WHO formula.
Other names | oral rehydration solution (ORS), oral rehydration salts (ORS), glucose-salt solution

Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially due to diarrhea.[1] It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium.[1] Oral rehydration therapy can also be given by a nasogastric tube.[1] Therapy can include the use of zinc supplements to reduce the duration of diarrhea in infants and children under the age of 5.[1] Use of oral rehydration therapy has been estimated to decrease the risk of death from diarrhea by up to 93%.[2]
Earliest known medication was done by Hemendra Nath Chatterjee in 1953 and he published it in The Lancet the results of using ORS to treat people with mild cholera.

Side effects may include vomiting, high blood sodium, or high blood potassium.[1] If vomiting occurs, it is recommended that use be paused for 10 minutes and then gradually restarted.[1] The recommended formulation includes sodium chloride, sodium citrate, potassium chloride, and glucose.[1] Glucose may be replaced by sucrose and sodium citrate may be replaced by sodium bicarbonate, if not available, although the resulting mixture is not shelf stable in high-humidity environments.[1][3] It works as glucose increases the uptake of sodium and thus water by the intestines, and the potassium chloride and sodium citrate help prevent hypokalemia and acidosis, respectively, which are both common side effects of diarrhea.[4][3][5] A number of other formulations are also available including versions that can be made at home.[4][2] However, the use of homemade solutions has not been well studied.[2]

Oral rehydration therapy was developed in the 1940s using electrolyte solutions with or without glucose on an empirical basis chiefly for mild or convalescent patients, but did not come into common use for rehydration and maintenance therapy until after the discovery that glucose promoted sodium and water absorption during cholera in the 1960s.[6] It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.[7] Globally, as of 2015, oral rehydration therapy is used by 41% of children with diarrhea.[8] This use has played an important role in reducing the number of deaths in children under the age of five.[8]

sources.text:
Commercially available oral rehydration salts:

left

, from Nepal;

right

, from Peru.

Commercially available ORS in water.

WHO and UNICEF have jointly developed official guidelines for the manufacture of oral rehydration solution and the oral rehydration salts used to make it (both often abbreviated ORS). They also describe other acceptable solutions, depending on material availability. Commercial preparations are available as prepared fluids and as packets of powder ready to mix with water.[16][17]

A basic oral rehydration therapy solution can also be prepared when packets of oral rehydration salts are not available.[18][19] The molar ratio of sugar to salt should be 1:1 and the solution should not be hyperosmolar.[20] The Rehydration Project states, "Making the mixture a little diluted (with more than 1 litre of clean water) is not harmful."[21]

The optimal fluid for preparing oral rehydration solution is clean water. However, if this is not available, the usually available water should be used. Oral rehydration solution should not be withheld simply because the available water is potentially unsafe; rehydration takes precedence.[22]

When oral rehydration salts packets and suitable teaspoons for measuring sugar and salt are not available, the WHO has recommended that homemade gruels, soups, etc., may be considered to help maintain hydration.[23] A Lancet review in 2013 emphasized the need for more research on appropriate home made fluids to prevent dehydration.[24] Sports drinks are not optimal oral rehydration solutions, but they can be used if optimal choices are not available. They should not be withheld for lack of better options; again, rehydration takes precedence. But they are not replacements for oral rehydration solutions in nonemergency situations.[25]

validation_inputs.draft:
**DO NOT WAIT TO MAKE A HOME REMEDY.** Your child's symptoms indicate **severe dehydration** and potential shock. Immediate professional medical help is required.

### 🚨 URGENT ACTION REQUIRED
1.  **Call emergency services immediately** or go to the nearest clinic/hospital. [S2]
    *   **Warning Signs Present:** Sleepiness (harder to wake than normal), inability to drink/keep fluids down, and no urine for 10 hours are critical signs of severe dehydration and shock. [S2][S1]
2.  **Do not delay** seeking help to prepare a home remedy or homemade solution. [S2]
3.  **Positioning:** While waiting for help, lay the child down. If there is no leg or spinal injury, raise their legs about 30 cm to aid circulation. Keep them warm with blankets and insulate them from the ground. [S7]

### Why Home Solutions Are Not Enough Now
*   **Severity:** The combination of extreme sleepiness ("very sleepy"), vomiting/inability to keep fluids down, and a lack of urine for over 10 hours signifies severe dehydration that requires intravenous fluids or advanced medical intervention. [S1][S2]
*   **Risk of Error:** Homemade solutions have not been well studied and can lead to dangerous imbalances (e.g., high blood sodium) if measurements are slightly off. Even when packets are unavailable, the priority in non-emergency settings is using tested commercial ORS; however, your child's condition is an emergency requiring professional care. [S3][S4]
*   **Ineffectiveness:** If the child cannot keep fluids down, oral rehydration alone may fail to reverse the rapid fluid loss. [S1]

### General Guidance for Mild Cases (NOT APPLICABLE HERE)
*If a child had mild diarrhea without these severe symptoms:*
*   The main measure is replacing fluids using Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS). [S1]
*   **Standard WHO Homemade Formula** (only if commercial ORS is unavailable and the patient can drink):
    *   1 liter of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled, or treated). [S1]
    *   6 level teaspoons of sugar (~25–30 g). [S1]
    *   ½ level teaspoon of salt (~2.5 g). [S1]
*   **Feeding:** Continue feeding (and breastfeeding) alongside rehydration. [S1]
*   **Zinc:** WHO recommends zinc for 10–14 days along with ORS for children, but dose must follow age-specific package inserts. [S1]

**Disclaimer:** This information does not replace a doctor's evaluation. Your child needs immediate professional assessment.

sources.text:
Oral rehydration therapy

Oral rehydration therapy
An oral rehydration solution (250ml) prepared according to WHO formula.
Other names | oral rehydration solution (ORS), oral rehydration salts (ORS), glucose-salt solution

Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially due to diarrhea.[1] It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium.[1] Oral rehydration therapy can also be given by a nasogastric tube.[1] Therapy can include the use of zinc supplements to reduce the duration of diarrhea in infants and children under the age of 5.[1] Use of oral rehydration therapy has been estimated to decrease the risk of death from diarrhea by up to 93%.[2]
Earliest known medication was done by Hemendra Nath Chatterjee in 1953 and he published it in The Lancet the results of using ORS to treat people with mild cholera.

Side effects may include vomiting, high blood sodium, or high blood potassium.[1] If vomiting occurs, it is recommended that use be paused for 10 minutes and then gradually restarted.[1] The recommended formulation includes sodium chloride, sodium citrate, potassium chloride, and glucose.[1] Glucose may be replaced by sucrose and sodium citrate may be replaced by sodium bicarbonate, if not available, although the resulting mixture is not shelf stable in high-humidity environments.[1][3] It works as glucose increases the uptake of sodium and thus water by the intestines, and the potassium chloride and sodium citrate help prevent hypokalemia and acidosis, respectively, which are both common side effects of diarrhea.[4][3][5] A number of other formulations are also available including versions that can be made at home.[4][2] However, the use of homemade solutions has not been well studied.[2]

Oral rehydration therapy was developed in the 1940s using electrolyte solutions with or without glucose on an empirical basis chiefly for mild or convalescent patients, but did not come into common use for rehydration and maintenance therapy until after the discovery that glucose promoted sodium and water absorption during cholera in the 1960s.[6] It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.[7] Globally, as of 2015, oral rehydration therapy is used by 41% of children with diarrhea.[8] This use has played an important role in reducing the number of deaths in children under the age of five.[8]

Commercially available oral rehydration salts:

left

, from Nepal;

right

, from Peru.

Commercially available ORS in water.

WHO and UNICEF have jointly developed official guidelines for the manufacture of oral rehydration solution and the oral rehydration salts used to make it (both often abbreviated ORS). They also describe other acceptable solutions, depending on material availability. Commercial preparations are available as prepared fluids and as packets of powder ready to mix with water.[16][17]

A basic oral rehydration therapy solution can also be prepared when packets of oral rehydration salts are not available.[18][19] The molar ratio of sugar to salt should be 1:1 and the solution should not be hyperosmolar.[20] The Rehydration Project states, "Making the mixture a little diluted (with more than 1 litre of clean water) is not harmful."[21]

The optimal fluid for preparing oral rehydration solution is clean water. However, if this is not available, the usually available water should be used. Oral rehydration solution should not be withheld simply because the available water is potentially unsafe; rehydration takes precedence.[22]

When oral rehydration salts packets and suitable teaspoons for measuring sugar and salt are not available, the WHO has recommended that homemade gruels, soups, etc., may be considered to help maintain hydration.[23] A Lancet review in 2013 emphasized the need for more research on appropriate home made fluids to prevent dehydration.[24] Sports drinks are not optimal oral rehydration solutions, but they can be used if optimal choices are not available. They should not be withheld for lack of better options; again, rehydration takes precedence. But they are not replacements for oral rehydration solutions in nonemergency situations.[25]

sources.section: Diarreia e desidratação — soro de reidratação oral
sources.text:
A diarreia mata principalmente por desidratação, sobretudo crianças. **A principal medida é repor líquidos.**

**Soro caseiro (quando não houver sais de reidratação oral – SRO – de farmácia/posto):**

- **1 litro de água potável** (fervida e fria ou tratada)
- **6 colheres de chá rasas de açúcar** (~25–30 g)
- **½ colher de chá rasa de sal** (~2,5 g)

Misture bem. O gosto não deve ser mais salgado que lágrimas. Ofereça goles pequenos e frequentes após cada evacuação. Faça novo a cada 24 horas.

- Continue alimentando (e amamentando bebês).
- **Crianças:** a OMS recomenda **zinco** por 10–14 dias junto com SRO (dose conforme idade e bula).
- Sinais de desidratação grave: muito sonolento, olhos fundos, pele que demora a voltar quando beliscada, não consegue beber, sem urina. **Busque atendimento urgente.**
- Diarreia com sangue, febre alta ou que dura mais de 2 semanas também precisa de avaliação.

> Fontes: WHO/UNICEF — *Oral Rehydration Salts: production of the new ORS* (2006) e *Clinical management of acute diarrhoea* (2004); Werner, D. — *Onde Não Há Médico*, "bebida de reidratação". Ministério da Saúde (Brasil) — manejo da diarreia aguda.

validation_inputs.draft:
**Não.** A situação descrita (sonolência excessiva, incapacidade de beber e ausência de urina por 10 horas) indica **desidratação grave** ou **choque**, exigindo atendimento médico urgente imediato. Não espere preparar a solução caseira para tentar tratar [S2].

### Passo a passo da ação:

1.  **Chame emergência imediatamente:** O estado "muito sonolento" e a dificuldade de acordar são sinais críticos de choque ou desidratação severa que requerem fluidos intravenosos (IV) e monitoramento hospitalar [S2].
2.  **Mantenha o conforto enquanto aguarda ajuda:**
    *   Deite a criança em uma superfície plana. Se não houver suspeita de trauma na coluna, eleve levemente as pernas (cerca de 30 cm) para melhorar o fluxo sanguíneo para órgãos vitais [S7].
    *   Aqueça a criança com cobertores para evitar perda de calor, já que pele fria e úmida é comum em choque [S7].
3.  **Não force líquidos por via oral agora:** Como a criança "não consegue reter líquidos" e está muito sonolenta, oferecer soro caseiro pode causar aspiração (engasgo) e não será suficiente para corrigir o quadro grave. A administração de fluidos deve ser feita em ambiente controlado [S5].
4.  **Leve ou espere a equipe médica:** Ao chegar ao hospital/UPA, informe que:
    *   Não houve urina há 10 horas.
    *   A criança está muito sonolenta e difícil de acordar.
    *   Houve diarreia recente.

### Sinais de alerta confirmados (Baseado nas fontes):
*   **Sonolência extrema/Dificuldade para acordar:** Indica choque ou desidratação grave; chame emergência imediatamente [S2].
*   **Não consegue beber/Não urina:** São sinais de desidratação grave que exigem intervenção médica urgente [S1].
*   **Ausência de urina por mais de 6-8 horas em crianças:** Sinal clássico de desidratação severa [S6].

> **Aviso importante:** A preparação de soro caseiro é uma medida para casos leves a moderados quando não há acesso a sais de reidratação oral (SRO) prontos, mas **não substitui** o tratamento hospitalar em casos graves como este. O uso de soro caseiro tem efeitos colaterais potenciais (como alteração nos níveis de sódio/potássio) e sua eficácia reduzida se não seguir rigorosamente as proporções da OMS [S3].

**Resumo:** A prioridade absoluta é transportar a criança ao serviço de saúde para reidratação intravenosa.

sources.text:
A diarreia mata principalmente por desidratação, sobretudo crianças. **A principal medida é repor líquidos.**

**Soro caseiro (quando não houver sais de reidratação oral – SRO – de farmácia/posto):**

- **1 litro de água potável** (fervida e fria ou tratada)
- **6 colheres de chá rasas de açúcar** (~25–30 g)
- **½ colher de chá rasa de sal** (~2,5 g)

Misture bem. O gosto não deve ser mais salgado que lágrimas. Ofereça goles pequenos e frequentes após cada evacuação. Faça novo a cada 24 horas.

- Continue alimentando (e amamentando bebês).
- **Crianças:** a OMS recomenda **zinco** por 10–14 dias junto com SRO (dose conforme idade e bula).
- Sinais de desidratação grave: muito sonolento, olhos fundos, pele que demora a voltar quando beliscada, não consegue beber, sem urina. **Busque atendimento urgente.**
- Diarreia com sangue, febre alta ou que dura mais de 2 semanas também precisa de avaliação.

request.q: Mi hijo de 2 años tiene diarrea, está muy somnoliento, no retiene líquidos y no ha orinado en 10 horas. ¿Puedo simplemente preparar una solución de rehidratación oral en casa?

results.answer:
**Fragmentos locales proporcionados.** Puede que no respalden toda la respuesta; las citas no se han verificado de forma independiente.

**NO.** No prepare ni administre la solución casera ahora mismo. Su hijo presenta signos de **deshidratación grave** y requiere atención médica urgente inmediatamente.

### 1. Señales de Alarma: Estado Crítico
Los síntomas que describe son peligrosos:
*   **Muy somnoliento:** Indica alteración del nivel de conciencia [2].
*   **No ha orinado en 10 horas:** Señal clara de fallo renal por deshidratación severa [2].
*   **No retiene líquidos (vómito):** Impide la rehidratación oral segura y aumenta el riesgo de shock [3].

> **Acción Inmediata:** Llámes a emergencias o diríjase al hospital más cercano. No retrase la búsqueda de ayuda para preparar un remedio casero, ya que estos signos pueden indicar choque [2].

### 2. Por qué no se puede tratar en casa ahora
*   **Riesgo de Shock:** La combinación de somnolencia y falta de orina sugiere inestabilidad hemodinámica [8].
*   **Incapacidad de tragar:** Si el niño "no retiene líquidos", existe alto riesgo de aspiración si se le fuerza a beber, incluso si está despierto. La terapia oral requiere una persona que pueda tragar con seguridad y estar despierta [3].
*   **Limitaciones del suero casero:** Aunque la fórmula casera es útil cuando no hay sales comerciales, su uso no está bien estudiado para casos graves y puede ser peligroso si el paciente vomita o tiene alteración mental [3].

### 3. Qué hacer mientras llega ayuda
Mientras se traslada al hospital:
1.  **Acueste a la persona:** Si no hay trauma en piernas o columna, eleve las piernas unos 30 cm para favorecer el retorno venoso [8].
2.  **Abriéguela:** Use cobijas y aíslela del suelo para evitar hipotermia [8].
3.  **Monitoreo:** Observe si la respiración se vuelve rápida o si la confusión aumenta; esto confirma la urgencia [8].

### Sin respaldo de fuentes locales: Contexto adicional
*   **OMS y Zinc:** Para casos leves o moderados, la OMS recomienda zinc durante 10–14 días junto con sales de rehidratación para reducir la duración de la diarrea en niños menores de 5 años [1]. Sin embargo, esto es un complemento al tratamiento médico, no un sustituto en situaciones de shock.
*   **Manejo del vómito:** Si el niño vomita durante la terapia oral (en casos leves), se recomienda pausar por 10 minutos y luego reanudar con sorbos pequeños [3]. En su caso actual, esto no aplica debido a la gravedad.

**Resumen:** Este es un caso de emergencia médica. La preparación de una solución casera es incorrecta y peligrosa en este momento. Priorice la seguridad y busque atención profesional inmediata.

> ⚠️ Orientación de primeros auxilios; no reemplaza la atención médica. Si hay ayuda disponible, búscala.

**NO.** No prepare ni administre la solución casera ahora mismo. Su hijo presenta signos de **deshidratación grave** y requiere atención médica urgente inmediatamente.

### 1. Señales de Alarma: Estado Crítico
Los síntomas que describe son peligrosos:
*   **Muy somnoliento:** Indica alteración del nivel de conciencia [S2].
*   **No ha orinado en 10 horas:** Señal clara de fallo renal por deshidratación severa [S2].
*   **No retiene líquidos (vómito):** Impide la rehidratación oral segura y aumenta el riesgo de shock [S3].

> **Acción Inmediata:** Llámes a emergencias o diríjase al hospital más cercano. No retrase la búsqueda de ayuda para preparar un remedio casero, ya que estos signos pueden indicar choque [S2].

### 2. Por qué no se puede tratar en casa ahora
*   **Riesgo de Shock:** La combinación de somnolencia y falta de orina sugiere inestabilidad hemodinámica [S8].
*   **Incapacidad de tragar:** Si el niño "no retiene líquidos", existe alto riesgo de aspiración si se le fuerza a beber, incluso si está despierto. La terapia oral requiere una persona que pueda tragar con seguridad y estar despierta [S3].
*   **Limitaciones del suero casero:** Aunque la fórmula casera es útil cuando no hay sales comerciales, su uso no está bien estudiado para casos graves y puede ser peligroso si el paciente vomita o tiene alteración mental [S3].

### 3. Qué hacer mientras llega ayuda
Mientras se traslada al hospital:
1.  **Acueste a la persona:** Si no hay trauma en piernas o columna, eleve las piernas unos 30 cm para favorecer el retorno venoso [S8].
2.  **Abriéguela:** Use cobijas y aíslela del suelo para evitar hipotermia [S8].
3.  **Monitoreo:** Observe si la respiración se vuelve rápida o si la confusión aumenta; esto confirma la urgencia [S8].

### Sin respaldo de fuentes locales: Contexto adicional
*   **OMS y Zinc:** Para casos leves o moderados, la OMS recomienda zinc durante 10–14 días junto con sales de rehidratación para reducir la duración de la diarrea en niños menores de 5 años [S1]. Sin embargo, esto es un complemento al tratamiento médico, no un sustituto en situaciones de shock.
*   **Manejo del vómito:** Si el niño vomita durante la terapia oral (en casos leves), se recomienda pausar por 10 minutos y luego reanudar con sorbos pequeños [S3]. En su caso actual, esto no aplica debido a la gravedad.

**Resumen:** Este es un caso de emergencia médica. La preparación de una solución casera es incorrecta y peligrosa en este momento. Priorice la seguridad y busque atención profesional inmediata.

sources.section: Diarrea y deshidratación — suero de rehidratación oral
sources.text:
La diarrea mata principalmente por deshidratación, sobre todo a los niños. **La medida principal es reponer líquidos.**

**Suero casero (cuando no haya sales de rehidratación oral – SRO – de farmacia/centro de salud):**

- **1 litro de agua potable** (hervida y fría o tratada)
- **6 cucharaditas rasas de azúcar** (~25–30 g)
- **½ cucharadita rasa de sal** (~2,5 g)

Mezcle bien. El sabor no debe ser más salado que las lágrimas. Ofrezca sorbos pequeños y frecuentes después de cada evacuación. Prepare uno nuevo cada 24 horas.

- Siga alimentando (y amamantando a los bebés).
- **Niños:** la OMS recomienda **zinc** durante 10–14 días junto con las SRO (dosis según la edad y el prospecto).
- Señales de deshidratación grave: muy somnoliento, ojos hundidos, piel que tarda en volver cuando se pellizca, no puede beber, sin orina. **Busque atención urgente.**
- La diarrea con sangre, fiebre alta o que dura más de 2 semanas también necesita evaluación.

> Fuentes: WHO/UNICEF — *Oral Rehydration Salts: production of the new ORS* (2006) y *Clinical management of acute diarrhoea* (2004); Werner, D. — *Donde no hay doctor*, "bebida de rehidratación". Ministério da Saúde (Brasil) — manejo de la diarrea aguda.
